いくつ ありますか — How many are there?
You count things and people with Japanese counters (ひとつ, ～まい, ～ほん, ～にん, ～さつ), say how long something takes (～じかん, ～にち) and shop with quantities.
There are four people in my family.
How long does it take to Japan?
I go to the pool three times a week.
To count things in general: ひとつ, ふたつ… とお.
To use the most common counters: ～まい, ～ほん, ～さつ, ～にん, ～ひき.
To put the number in the right place: りんご を みっつ ください.
To say how many times you do something (～かい) and how long it takes (～じかん, ～にち).
To shop at the post office and the market.
Kenji wants to send his wife in Hiroshima a parcel for her birthday. Mihai goes with him to the post office, then to the market.
Mihai, I’m sending my wife a present. Won’t you come with me to the post office?
Two Spanish books, three T-shirts and two bottles of olive oil.
How long does it take by air?
About a week. By sea it takes two months.
Her birthday is on the tenth, so by air, please. And five stamps and an envelope, please.
(At the market) Kenji, is this the shopping for the restaurant?
Yes. Excuse me, six of these fish and ten tomatoes, please.
Certainly. And lemons? Three for a euro.
Kenji, how many times a week do you come to the market?
Five times. Every morning I shop for about an hour.
my wife (“tsuma ni” = to my wife)
The counter ～ほん changes: いっぽん (1), にほん (2), さんぼん (3), よんほん (4), ろっぽん (6), はっぽん (8), じゅっぽん (10). Don’t learn them all today, just 1, 2 and 3!
For 1 and 2 people there are special words: ひとり, ふたり. From 3 onwards it’s regular: さんにん, よにん (⚠️ not “yonnin”), ごにん.
The っ pause before “tsu”: mit-tsu, yot-tsu, mut-tsu. Without the pause it sounds wrong.
1. The “old Japanese” numbers: ひとつ… とお
Japanese has TWO sets of numbers. いち, に, さん (chapter 2) are for prices, times and dates. To count THINGS in general there’s an old set, from 1 to 10:
This set works for almost anything: apples, eggs, boxes, questions. If you don’t know the special counter, use this one, everyone will understand you!
The question: いくつ ですか (how many?). Above 10, use the ordinary numbers: じゅういち, じゅうに…

In Japanese, as in Chinese, you put a “counting word” after the number, depending on the SHAPE of the thing. It’s like English “three SHEETS of paper”, “two BOTTLES of oil”, except that it’s compulsory:
きって, T シャツ, きっぷ, かみ (paper)
You’ve already seen it in chapter 3: いっぴき, さんびき, よんひき. ～ひき changes its sound too, just like ～ほん.
This is the biggest difference from English. The number with its counter comes AFTER the particle を (or が), right before the verb:
English speakers say “みっつ の りんご を かいました” (translating “three apples”). It’s understood, but sounds unnatural. Japanese order: THING を NUMBER VERB.
“X times a week” = PERIOD に NUMBER: いっしゅうかん に さんかい (three times a week).
For duration, use the verb かかります (it takes / it costs): にほん まで じゅうよじかん かかります (It takes 14 hours to Japan).
Don’t confuse: いちじ = one O’CLOCK (chapter 4), いちじかん = ONE HOUR (duration).
5. Days of the month (the first ten)
Days 1–10 have special names, also used for “X days” (except 1):
See the similarity with ひとつ, ふたつ…? ふつか ~ ふたつ, みっか ~ みっつ. From 11 it’s regular: じゅういちにち. Exceptions to remember: はつか (20) and じゅうよっか (14).
How many books is Kenji sending?
T シャツ を なんまい おくります か。
How long does the parcel take by air?
How many lemons does Kenji buy?
つま から の てがみ — A letter from his wife
A week later, Kenji receives a letter from his wife, Haruka, in Hiroshima.
To Kenji. Thank you for the parcel! It arrived on the eighth.
I read the two books straight away. Because Spanish is difficult, I used a dictionary.
I love all three T-shirts. Our daughter said she wants one too.
I gave one bottle of olive oil to our neighbour, Mrs Yamada.
We’re fine here. We have three dogs. And a kitten has arrived too!
Our daughter does piano four times a week.
You’re coming home for a month in August, aren’t you? We’re all waiting for you.
from (at the end of a letter)
What did Haruka do with one bottle of oil?
She gave it to the neighbour
How many animals do they have now in total?
How long is Kenji staying at home in August?
ひみつ の りょこう — The secret trip
At the beginning of March, Kenji told the club members a secret.
“The tenth next week is my wife’s birthday. I’m going back to Hiroshima. But she doesn’t know.”
On the eighth he leaves Madrid, fourteen hours by plane. On the ninth he arrives in Tokyo.
From Tokyo, four hours by shinkansen. On the morning of the tenth he arrives in Hiroshima.
He stays in Hiroshima for five days. Then he goes back to Madrid again.
Sofia raised her hand. “I will! I’ll make pizza and pasta!”
“Because it’s only five days, the menu can turn a little Italian,” Kenji laughed.
All the club members chose the presents together.
Ana bought two Spanish plates. They’re blue and beautiful.
Mihai brought three jars of Romanian honey.
Carlos, a flamenco CD. Hanako, a book.
Yuki took a photo of all twelve of them. Everyone is smiling.
On the morning of the eighth, everyone went to the airport. Kenji had two bags.
One with clothes, the other with everyone’s presents.
“Have a good trip! Say hello to your wife!”
The tenth, seven in the morning. Kenji is standing in front of a small house in Hiroshima.
Dogs can be heard from the house. One, two, three…
The door opened. It was Haruka. She was holding a cup of tea.
Haruka didn’t say anything. She dropped the tea.
The three dogs and the kitten came running too. The house was full of noise.
That evening, Kenji took out the presents one by one.
Two plates, three jars of honey, a CD, a book.
Finally, a photo. “These are my friends in Madrid. There are twelve of them.”
Haruka looked at the photo for a long time.
“You have lots of good friends. Next time I want to come to Madrid too.”
Kenji smiled and answered: “Next time, all three of us will go.”
hand (“te o agemashita” = raised her hand)
have a good trip (to someone leaving)
How many days does Kenji stay in Hiroshima?
What did Haruka do when she saw Kenji?
Fill in with the correct number and counter. You can write in kana or romaji.
I go to the gym twice a week.
There are three people in my family.
Text to read: Yuki’s shopping list
Yuki is preparing dinner for the club and makes a list.
There are twelve people in the club in total.
I’m buying twelve eggs, five carrots, three onions.
Rice, five kilos. Paper plates, twenty.
Six bottles of juice and four of tea.
The cooking takes about three hours. I’ll ask Kenji to help me!

How many people are in the club?

Write 8–10 sentences: how many people there are in your family, what pets you have, what’s on your desk (how many books, pens, notebooks), how many times a week you do something (sport, shopping, Japanese), how long your journey to work or school takes. Leave spaces between words.
I used at least 3 different counters (～まい, ～ほん, ～さつ, ～にん, ～ひき).
I put the number AFTER を / が, before the verb.
I used ～かい with いっしゅうかん に.
I used ～じかん or ～ぷん with かかります.
I used ひとつ / ふたつ / みっつ for an ordinary thing.
There are four people in my family. We have a dog.
There are five books and three pens on my desk.
I study Japanese five times a week.
It takes thirty minutes by bus to get to the office.
